mcqs.question: Which of the following symbols correctly represents the conjunction of two statements P and Q?
mcqs.explanation: The conjunction (AND) of P and Q is denoted by P ∧ Q and is true only when both P and Q are true. Option B is disjunction, C is implication, and D is biconditional.

mcqs.question: The compound statement ‘P or Q’ (P ∨ Q) is false only when:

options.A: Both P and Q are true
options.B: Both P and Q are false
options.C: At least one of P or Q is true
options.D: Exactly one of P or Q is true

mcqs.answer: Both P and Q are false
mcqs.explanation: A disjunction is true if at least one component is true; it becomes false only when both components are false. Hence option B is correct. All other options describe situations where the disjunction is true.

mcqs.question: In the implication P → Q, the statement is false only when:

options.A: P is true and Q is false
options.B: Both P and Q are true
options.C: Both P and Q are false

mcqs.answer: P is true and Q is false
mcqs.explanation: An implication is false only in the case where the antecedent (P) is true while the consequent (Q) is false. In all other cases (both true, both false, or P false) the implication is considered true.

mcqs.question: Which of the following expressions is logically equivalent to the biconditional P ↔ Q?
mcqs.explanation: A biconditional is true when both statements have the same truth value—both true or both false. The expression (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q) captures exactly those two cases. Options B, C, and D represent conjunction, disjunction, and implication respectively, not the biconditional.

mcqs.question: Consider the compound statement (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬R. Which of the following assignments of truth values makes the whole statement true?

options.A: P = True, Q = False, R = False
options.B: P = False, Q = False, R = True
options.C: P = False, Q = True, R = True
options.D: P = True, Q = True, R = True

mcqs.answer: P = True, Q = False, R = False
mcqs.explanation: First evaluate P ∨ Q: with P true and Q false, the result is true. ¬R is true because R is false. Hence (true) ∧ (true) = true, so the compound statement is true. In options B, C, and D either the disjunction is false or ¬R is false, making the whole statement false.

mcqs.question: Let P denote ‘It is raining’ and Q denote ‘It is windy’. In which scenario is the conjunction P ∧ Q true?

options.A: It is raining but not windy.
options.B: It is windy but not raining.
options.C: Both it is raining and it is windy.
options.D: Neither it is raining nor it is windy.

mcqs.answer: Both it is raining and it is windy.
mcqs.explanation: A conjunction P ∧ Q is true only when both component statements are true simultaneously. Scenario C satisfies both conditions. All other scenarios have at least one false component, making the conjunction false.

mcqs.question: A common misconception is that ‘P or Q’ is false when both P and Q are true. Which of the following correctly states the truth value of the disjunction when both P and Q are true?

options.D: The truth value depends on the context.

mcqs.explanation: In classical logic, the inclusive ‘or’ (P ∨ Q) is true if at least one of the statements is true, including the case where both are true. Therefore option A is correct; the other options reflect the misconception or irrelevant considerations.

mcqs.question: If a number is divisible by 4 (P) then it is even (Q). Which of the following statements is a logically valid conclusion derived from this implication?

options.A: If a number is odd, then it is not divisible by 4.
options.B: If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4.
options.C: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4.
options.D: If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is odd.

mcqs.answer: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4.
mcqs.explanation: The contrapositive of P → Q is ¬Q → ¬P, which is logically equivalent to the original implication. Here, ¬Q means ‘not even’ and ¬P means ‘not divisible by 4’, giving option C. Option A is not guaranteed (an odd number could be divisible by 4? actually impossible, but it is not the direct contrapositive). Option B and D are not valid deductions from the given implication.
